title: Над 48.000 лица се регистрирале за гласање во странство на општите избори во Босна и Херцеговина
content:
Над 48.000 лица се регистрирале за гласање во странство на општите избори во Босна и Херцеговина
- Од вкупно 48.078 регистрирани избирачи надвор од земјата, 45.457 одлучиле да гласаат по пошта, додека 2.621 лице гласачкото право ќе го остварат во дипломатско-конзуларните претставништва.
Сараево, 19 август 2026 (МИА) – Повеќе од 48.000 лица се регистрирале за гласање во странство за општите избори во Босна и Херцеговина, соопшти Централната изборна комисија на БиХ (ЦИК), а пренесе националната телевизија БХРТ.
Од вкупно 48.078 регистрирани избирачи надвор од земјата, 45.457 одлучиле да гласаат по пошта, додека 2.621 лице гласачкото право ќе го остварат во дипломатско-конзуларните претставништва.
ЦИК одби околу 5.000 барања за регистрација во странство поради неисполнување на законските услови. По поднесените 39 жалби, комисијата прифати четири, додека останатите беа отфрлени од Судот на Босна и Херцеговина како неосновани.
На претстојните избори се очекува правото на глас да го остварат околу 3,4 милиони граѓани. Избирачите ќе ги избираат тројцата членови на Претседателството на Босна и Херцеговина, повеќе од 500 пратеници во Парламентарното собрание на БиХ и во парламентите на двата ентитета – Република Српска и Федерацијата Босна и Херцеговина, како и пратеници во кантоналните собранија.
Според Дејтонскиот мировен договор од 1995 година, со кој заврши војната во БиХ, државата е составена од два ентитета – Република Српска, со претежно српско население, и Федерацијата Босна и Херцеговина, во која мнозинството го чинат Бошњаците и Хрватите.
Ентитетите имаат сопствени влади, парламенти и полициски сили, но се поврзани преку централните државни институции, меѓу кои се правосудството, вооружените сили, безбедносните служби и даночната администрација. Дејтонскиот договор ја дефинира и улогата на високиот претставник на меѓународната заедница, кој располага со овластувања за наметнување закони и за разрешување функционери. ссм/

title: Best evidence summary of non-pharmacological interventions for postoperative abdominal distension in gynecological laparoscopic
content: ObjectiveTo retrieve and summarize the best evidence on non-pharmacological interventions for postoperative bloating in gynecological laparoscopic patients, providing an evidence-based foundation for the clinical management of gastrointestinal function.MethodsAccording to the 5S pyramid model of evidence-based practice resources, a systematic search was conducted in databases such as Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, PubMed, CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP. Relevant guidelines, clinical decision, evidence summaries, systematic reviews, and expert consensus were collected. The search period spanned from the inception of the databases to January 31, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened and evaluated the literature, followed by evidence extraction and summarization according to the JBI Evidence Grading and Recommendation System.ResultA total of 20 articles were included, comprising 4 guidelines, 1 clinical decision, 5 expert consensus, 1 evidence summary, and 9 systematic reviews. By summarizing and integrating the evidence, 23 best pieces of evidence were formed from 8 aspects: preoperative prevention, posture management, early activity, nutritional intervention, chewing gum, beverage intervention, appropriate traditional Chinese medicine techniques, and health education.ConclusionThis study summarizes the best evidence for non-pharmacological intervention of postoperative abdominal distension after gynecological laparoscopy from eight aspects. This evidence summary possesses high scientific rigor and clinical applicability, providing guidance for medical staff in constructing standardized postoperative abdominal distension management protocols, thereby facilitating the improvement of patients’ postoperative recovery experience. However, the findings are based on previously published evidence and have not been prospectively validated in clinical practice; therefore, the recommendations should be adapted to local clinical contexts and further evaluated in implementation studies.Systematic Review Registrationhttp://ebn.nursing.fudan.edu.cn/home, identifier ES202610098.

title: Migration is reshaping life for married women in Senegal
content:
Migration is reshaping life for married women in Senegal
Loading...
| Léona, Senegal
A plastic chair, a floor mat, a washbasin. In a sandy courtyard in this rural community in northwestern Senegal, that is all it takes to conjure an imaginary house as part of a women’s program performed for a community radio station.
“Focus ... action,” calls out Seydina Alioune Gueye, the program’s director. The few spectators who have gathered at the scene fall silent, and the actresses take their places. One actress mimics exhaustion as she folds invisible laundry. Nearby, another actress prepares a meal. At the center of the courtyard, Mr. Gueye portrays a domineering husband. He looks for a pair of trousers, raises his voice, accuses. Slowly, the plot unfolds: He stirs conflict between the two women to justify taking a third wife – a woman who is already pregnant. The scene feels familiar to the actresses and the audience.
“We act what we see,” actress Khadi Dièye says after the performance. “We talk about forced marriages, violence, irregular migration. These are our realities.”
Why We Wrote This
In Léona, as in much of the surrounding Louga region, migration structures lives, expectations, and imaginations. It also sustains a local economy heavily dependent on remittances – income that supports many rural households, especially women.
Beside her, actress Mame Bintou, nods. “We want to denounce,” she says, “but also make people think.”
The weekly radio program is a space for women to discuss the men who have left and the challenges of living without them. Taking up to four wives is legal in Senegal, though the practice is a common source of tension discussed on the women’s program.
Many men here go abroad to work and send money home. Nearly 60% of those men migrate to Europe; most of the rest go elsewhere in Africa, according to data from the Reception, Orientation, and Monitoring Office (BAOS), a Senegalese government entity supporting migrants and their families. Often, the men marry just before departing and do not return for years. The women are typically sent to live with in-laws.
In Léona, as in much of the surrounding Louga region, migration structures lives, expectations, and imaginations. It also sustains a local economy heavily dependent on remittances – income that supports many rural households, especially women.
Some describe a life close to confinement. There is fear of gossip, fear of judgment.
“You have to be careful about everything,” Mariama Achemya Aïdara whispers, saying she felt constantly watched by her in-laws. Going out, working, moving around. Every gesture can be commented on.
So they gather.
At the center of Léona, a mud house topped by a tall antenna hosts the radio station. “Here, women can talk about what they really live through,” says Matel Ba, the station’s director since 2018.
In a community scattered across more than 100 hamlets, the station connects people and fosters dialogue. On the Saturday morning women’s program, the stories are often the same: absent husbands, unreliable remittances, disagreements with in-laws, and, for some, domestic violence. “Some women live alone for 20 years,” Ms. Ba says. “How do you build a life under those conditions?”
Sometimes, the radio acts as a mediator. Ms. Ba has even gone to meet husbands to hear their side when they return home. But she also promotes employment training programs, economic projects, and paths toward independence for the women.
A few streets away from the radio station, about 30 women gather for a tontine, a rotating savings group common across West Africa. Sitting in a circle, they each place a small amount of cash into a metal box. “It helps us not depend only on men,” explains Ms. Aïdara. The fund finances small businesses and community projects.
Without the men, caring for everything – the fields, the houses, the children – falls to the women. In the Niayes, fertile coastal lowlands between sand dunes and the Atlantic Ocean, two women rake the soil side by side amid a light breeze off the water. Moisture trapped in the ground allows finicky crops such as onions and peanuts to grow. Goats wander past, and children run nearby.
The women live together in a large house built with money sent from Europe. Around them, other buildings rise from the sand, some still unfinished. Salimata Boye occupies one of these homes. Her husband has been in Spain since 2006, and returns only once every two years. In the meantime, she works in the fields, under the watchful eyes of her brother-in-law. Even going out requires permission.
Beside her, her sister-in-law Yama Soul raises her three children alone. Her husband also left by boat years ago. “I would prefer him to be here,” she says quietly.
Despite the difficulties of long-distance marriage, a husband abroad is still widely seen as a marker of success and social mobility. Among the new generation, though, attitudes are gradually changing.
At dusk, 19-year-old Seynabou Tabane prepares chicken yassa with her mother and sister. She says a long-distance marriage is not for her. “I don’t like it,” she says. She wants something different: “Someone who supports me, trusts me, and helps me with my projects.” She adds that she dreams of becoming a veterinarian.
Her mother, Maimouna Sougou, listens quietly. She knows the subject well, having herself endured a long-distance marriage. She discusses these very issues every week on the radio, where she is one of the hosts. The younger women continue those conversations on social media, with friends, at the gym, or by the sea.
In Léona, women are carving out new spaces to talk. And little by little, they are finding their voice and their place.

title: Proteome-Wide Antigen Discovery Reveals Compartment-Specific Humoral Responses in Coccidioidomycosis
content: Coccidioidomycosis is a fungal infection of rising public health concern, with coccidioidal meningitis (CM) representing its most devastating manifestation. Diagnosis of CM remains challenging due to the limited sensitivity and technical demands of conventional cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) serology testing. To comprehensively characterize the humoral immune response across the full spectrum of coccidioidal disease, we designed and deployed a proteome-wide Coccidioides phage immunoprecipitation sequencing (PhIP-Seq) library tiling both C. immitis and C. posadasii proteomes. We profiled antibody reactivity in sera from 323 participants spanning six clinically defined disease severity categories, as well as CSF and matched serum from participants with confirmed CM (n=108) and Coccidioides-negative other neurologic disease (OND) controls (n=163). Serum profiling revealed a potential narrowing of the antigenic repertoire as disease severity increased, with subclinical participants mounting the broadest response (55 peptides from 55 proteins) compared to 3-7 peptides in symptomatic categories. Two proteins, spherule outer wall glycoprotein (SOWgp) and a previously uncharacterized Proline-rich Immunodominant Antigen (PIA1), emerged as immunodominant across disease categories. Enriched antigens were disproportionately proline-rich and repetitive, a structural feature associated with immunodominance in other pathogens. CSF profiling revealed a compartment-specific antibody signature in CM, with 94% of CSF-enriched seroreactive peptides absent from matched sera. To orthogonally validate these findings, we developed a five-antigen Luminex assay using SOWgp- and PIA1-derived peptides, achieving 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity in both a discovery cohort (CM n=20, OND n=20) and an independent, blinded validation cohort (34 CM and 36 OND CSF samples. These findings expand the repertoire of Coccidioides serological responses associated with disease severity and demonstrate that proteome-wide antibody discovery can be translated into a targeted, high-performance diagnostic platform.

27일 외교부 당국자에 따르면 전날 네팔 라수와 지역에서 발생한 홍수로 연락이 두절된 한국남동발전과 두산에너빌리티 소속 국민 9명은 사고 당시 한국인 직원들이 주로 쓰는 숙소와 사무실에 있었다.
상대적으로 지대가 낮은 이 지역은 홍수의 직접적인 피해를 당하였고, 수력발전소 건설을 위해 여기서 일하던 국민 9명의 소재는 아직 불분명하다.
외교부 당국자는 "발전소도 거의 다 쓸려내려 갔다고 한다. 연락두절된 분들이 계셨던 건물도 유실됐다고 한다"고 말했다.
반면 홍수로 고립되긴 했으나 안전한 상태로 구조를 기다릴 수 있었던 국민 10명은 주로 현지인 직원들이 근무하고 숙소로 쓰는 '파워하우스'라는 장소에 있었다.
홍수가 발생한 지역과 거리가 있고, 평소 직원들이 숙식하는 곳이라 물과 식자재도 있었다. 현장에 파견된 주네팔대사관 소속 영사가 이들을 직접 확인한 결과 외견상 건강에 이상은 없었다.
다만 홍수 때문에 주변 도로가 유실돼 그 지역에서 벗어날 방도가 없어 헬기 구조를 기다릴 수밖에 없었다.
외교부 당국자는 "파워하우스는 하천지역에서 어느 정도 떨어져 있고 지대가 더 높다고 한다. 그래서 피해를 안 당한 것"이라고 설명했다.
파워하우스에 있던 국민 10명 중 9명은 이날 네팔 당국이 헬기를 이용해 안전한 지역으로 이송했다.
파워하우스 지역에는 국민 10명뿐만 아니라 다른 외국인과 현지인 등 수백명이 같이 고립돼 있었는데 네팔 당국이 운용할 수 있는 헬기 수가 제한돼 대피가 순차적으로 이뤄지면서 구조에 시간이 걸렸다고 한다.
9명도 한번에 헬기를 타고 나오지 못하고 4번에 걸쳐 구조됐다.
남은 1명은 두산에너빌리티 소속 현장소장인데 그는 네팔인 직원 15명이 구조될 때까지 남겠다고 했으며, 이에 영사와 대사관 행정직원도 같이 남았다.
사고 당시 현장에는 한국인 총 28명이 있었다.
두산에너빌리티 직원 21명 중 6명이 연락두절됐고, 10명은 파워하우스에 있었으며, 5명은 마침 휴가였다.
남동발전 소속 7명 중 4명은 무사했고, 3명이 연락두절 상태다.

구조·수색은 현재 네팔 군과 경찰이 하는데 험준한 산악 지형이라 야간에는 수색작업이 전혀 안 되고 일출 후, 일몰 전까지만 되는 상황이라고 외교부 당국자는 설명했다.
정부는 이날 외교부, 경찰청, 소방청 인원 총 11명으로 구성된 신속대응팀을 현지로 파견했지만, 대응팀은 현지시간 밤늦게야 도착할 예정이다.
공항이 위치한 네팔 카트만두에서 사고 지역까지 육로로 이동이 어려워 헬기 등 대체 이동 수단을 확보해야 하는 어려움도 있다.
신속대응팀은 인력 규모나 보유 장비 등을 고려하면 직접 구조·수색 활동을 벌이기보다는 일단 현장 상황을 파악하고, 네팔 당국의 협조를 구하는 데 주력할 방침이다.
외교부 당국자는 "신속대응팀장이 네팔 고위당국자를 접촉해서 한국민에 대해 특별한 협조를 요청할 것으로 알고 있다"고 말했다.
정부는 신속대응팀이 파악한 현장 여건 등을 고려해 구조대를 추가로 보낼 것으로 예상된다.
조현 외교부 장관은 이날 네팔 외교장관과 통화에서 수색·구조 관련 협조를 구하면서 해외긴급구호대의 신속한 파견도 검토·추진해 나가겠다고 했다.
해외긴급구호대는 통상 다른 나라에서 재난재해가 발생할 경우 인도적 지원 차원에서 파견하는 데, 이번에 파견될 경우 한국인 수색·구조도 병행할 전망이다.
다만 정부가 해외긴급구호대를 파견하려면 네팔 정부의 동의가 필요하다.
한편 이번 사고를 현지에서 일차적으로 대응하는 주네팔대사관은 최근 인사 발령으로 대사가 공석이며, 행정직원을 제외한 공무원은 조아름 대사대리를 포함해 총 6명이다.
아울러 정부는 통상 연 2만명 정도의 한국인이 관광 목적으로 네팔을 방문하는 점을 고려해 이번 홍수 피해자가 추가로 있을 가능성에도 촉각을 곤두세우고 있다.
네팔관광청이 이날 12시 기준으로 발표한 외국인 관광객 실종자 통계에 한국인은 없었다.

title: Dviračiai užims Vilnių: sekmadienį vyks „Velomaratono“ varžybos
content:
Šį sekmadienį, rugpjūčio 23-ąją, Vilnius vienai dienai taps dviratininkų miestu – į 17-ąjį „Velomaratoną“ sostinės gatvėse išriedės beveik 10 tūkstančių dviračių entuziastų, rašoma organizatorių pranešime žiniasklaidai.
Didžiausioje Baltijos šalyse dviračių fiestoje jėgas išbandys profesionalai, mėgėjai ir vaikai, o į trasą leisis ne tik dviratininkai, bet ir paspirtukų, riedlenčių bei riedučių entuziastai.
„Velomaratonas“ – tai ne tik varžybos dėl greičiausio rato ar aukščiausio rezultato. Tai diena, kai sportas susitinka su bendryste, o fizinis iššūkis – su gera emocija. Čia svarbios ne tik sekundės ir kilometrai, bet ir žmonės, su kuriais dalijamasi trasa, palaikymas prie finišo ir jausmas, kurį išsineši dar ilgai po renginio.
Velomaratono čempionė Daiva Ragažinskienė: „Šio renginio tiesiog negaliu praleisti“
Tarp šių metų „Velomaratono“ dalyvių – ir viena stipriausių Lietuvos moterų grupės dviratininkių Daiva Ragažinskienė. Renginyje ji dalyvauja nuo 2021-ųjų ir jau ne kartą įrodė savo meistriškumą – pergalę iškovojo 2021, 2023 ir 2024 metais.
2022-aisiais kovą jai teko nutraukti anksčiau laiko, kai trasoje prakiuro padanga, o praėjusiais metais Daiva prieš startą dėl lietaus buvo beveik nusprendusi nedalyvauti. Vis dėlto ji ryžosi stoti į trasą ir, nepaisydama sudėtingų oro sąlygų, apgynė čempionės titulą.
Šiemet jos pavardė taip pat įrašyta tarp dalyvių, nors sprendimą startuoti sportininkė priėmė ne iš karto.
„Šiemet į „Velomaratoną“ užsiregistravau gana anksti, tačiau po viso sezono jaučiu šiokį tokį nuovargį, todėl kurį laiką dvejojau – dalyvauti ar vis dėlto savaitgalį skirti poilsiui namuose. Visgi šiuo metu jaučiuosi pakankamai gerai, o trenerio paskatinta nusprendžiau – starte būsiu.
„Velomaratonas“ man nėra vien varžybos. Tai žmonių susibūrimas, draugų susitikimas ir tikra dviračių sporto šventė miestui. Tokio būrio dviračių entuziastų turbūt nesutraukia nė vienas kitas dviračių renginys Lietuvoje, todėl kiekvienais metais atrodo, kad jo tiesiog negaliu praleisti“, – dalinasi profesionalios dviratininkės karjerą baigusi Daiva Ragažinskienė.
Kai Vilniaus gatvės priklauso dviratininkams
Vienas išskirtiniausių „Velomaratono“ potyrių – galimybė Vilnių pamatyti kitaip. Startavę Nepriklausomybės aikštėje, mėgėjų ir sportinių važiavimų dalyviai mins Gedimino prospektu, Šventaragio, Arsenalo, Žvejų ir Upės gatvėmis, per Žvėryno tiltą bei A. Goštauto gatve.
Šią dieną įprastai automobiliams skirtos sostinės gatvės trumpam tampa dviratininkų trasa, o miestas – gerokai ramesnis ir kitoks nei įprastai. Galimybė važiuoti per Vilniaus centrą, pamatyti įprastai nenutylančias gatves be automobilių ir atrasti pažįstamas vietas iš naujo – viena iš patirčių, dėl kurių dalyviai į „Velomaratoną“ sugrįžta kasmet.
Ne tik lenktynės, bet ir visa diena, skirta šeimai ir draugams
„Velomaratonas“ – ne tik sportinės varžybos, bet ir visos dienos judėjimo šventė, į kurią kviečiami dalyviai, jų šeimos, draugai. Organizatoriai siekia, kad veiklos čia rastų kiekvienas – nuo sportinių iššūkių, viktorinų ir edukacijų iki vaikams skirtų pramogų, dviračių akrobatų pasirodymų ir muzikos.
„Norime, kad žmonės į „Velomaratoną“ ateitų ne tik startuoti, bet ir praleistų čia visą dieną drauge. Tai šventė, kurioje svarbi ne tik finišo linija, bet ir pats buvimas, judėjimas bei bendrystė“, – sako „Velomaratono“ organizatoriai.
17 metų – ir vis didesnė bendruomenė
Šiemet „Velomaratonas“ vyks jau 17-ąjį kartą. Per šiuos metus renginys tapo viena svarbiausių Lietuvos dviračių bendruomenės tradicijų, kasmet į Vilnių suburiančia tūkstančius dalyvių iš įvairių Lietuvos miestų ir užsienio.
„Stebėti, kaip per 17 metų auga ir stiprėja dviračių bendruomenė, mums – didelė privilegija. Savotiška paauglystė, bet drauge ir didžiulė branda. Kasmet matome vis daugiau dalyvių, besiryžtančių išbandyti jėgas sportiniuose važiavimuose, vis daugiau mėgėjų, kurie sugrįžta jau su visa šeima ir Velomaratono sekmadieniui ruošia ypatingus kostiumus, puošiasi.
Stebint visus dalyvius kasmet apima labai paprastas, bet svarbus jausmas – prasmė. Džiaugiamės galėdami auginti bendruomenę, kuriai rūpi šeima, sveikas gyvenimo būdas, eismo saugumas ir tvarumas“, – sako „Velomaratono“ organizatoriai.
Rugpjūčio 23-ąją Vilnius vėl priklausys dviratininkams. Vieniems tai bus kova dėl geriausio rezultato, kitiems – pirmasis rimtesnis iššūkis, dar kitiems – smagus sekmadienis su šeima ar draugais. Tačiau visus juos vienys viena kryptis – pirmyn.

title: Janine Mathias e GOG e sobem ao palco do Teatro Paiol neste final de semana
content:
Celebrando 14 anos de trajetória artística em Curitiba, Janine Mathias recebe Genival Oliveira Gonçalves, o GOG, rapper, cantor e escritor brasileiro, que faz parte da primeira geração do rap, reconhecido nacionalmente como o “Poeta do Rap Nacional”. Os shows acontecem neste sábado (15) e domingo (16).
Nascida em Brasília e radicada em Curitiba desde 2008, a cantora, compositora e produtora cultural construiu uma carreira marcada pela valorização da ancestralidade e da cultura negra. Agora, ela divide o palco com GOG, artista cuja obra se tornou referência pela potência poética e crítica social, em um espetáculo que une música, memória e resistência.
O primeiro encontro aconteceu na noite desta sexta-feira (14), com um bate-papo no Conservatório de MPB de Curitiba. Na conversa, GOG expressou sua felicidade em estar na capital paranaense e reforçou sua concepção de que a periferia “pode criar realidades diferentes”. “Se periferia é periferia em qualquer lugar, então não é por acaso”, afirmou. Janine e GOG conversaram com o público sobre formação social brasileira, cultura e educação. O consenso do debate apontou a cultura hip hop como continuidade da resistência ancestral.
A comemoração continua neste fim de semana, com duas apresentações de Janine Mathias e GOG no Teatro Paiol: neste sábado (15) e domingo (16), às 20h e 19h, respectivamente. Os ingressos podem ser comprados no site ou na bilheteria.

title: Rekordni broj posjetitelja na neobičnoj plaži u Trstu. Muški i ženski dio dijeli zid
content:
Hit plaža u Trstu obara rekorde. Muškarci i žene kupaju se odvojeno
KUPALIŠTE u Trstu na kojem su muški i ženski dio odvojeni zidom ove je godine ostvarilo rekordan rezultat, a lokalni list Il Piccolo piše da su tome ponajviše pridonijele žene, koje plažu posjećuju u većem broju od muškaraca. Plažu je u samo tri mjeseca posjetilo više od 100 tisuća ljudi, točnije njih 106.696, uz ukupan prihod od približno 120.000 eura.
Ulaznica je jeftinija od vožnje autobusom
Poslovanje plaže Pedocin pokazuje vrlo dobre rezultate bez obzira na to promatraju li se podaci iz društvene ili ekonomske perspektive. Dnevna ulaznica za kupalište Alla Lanterna stoji 1.20 eura, manje od vožnje autobusom. No tajna uspjeha nije u cijeni, nego u održavanju tradicije koja seže još u vrijeme Habsburgovaca.
Zid između muškaraca i žena dug je 74 metra
Habsburgovci su između muškog i ženskog dijela plaže podignuli zid dug 74 metra. Takav tip plaže privlači brojne turiste zbog iskustva koje je jedinstveno u Europi. Il Piccolo piše da Pedocin uglavnom posjećuju žene. Samo u srpnju prodano je 53.610 ulaznica, u usporedbi s 34.885 u 2025. i 40.160 u 2024. godini.
U svibnju, prvom mjesecu u kojem se počeo naplaćivati ulaz, prodano je 17.035 ulaznica. U istom mjesecu 2025. prodano ih je 10.315, a 2024. godine 7393. U brojke je uključen i besplatan ulaz za djecu mlađu od 12 godina te posjetitelje s invaliditetom u pratnji. Novine ističu da je objektu potrebna obnova.

title: Hyrox, Deka, Athx, Hyatlón... el boom de las pruebas híbridas que mezclan running y crossfit: "Es muy instagrameable"
content:
Un pabellón enorme lleno de gente, música alta, una línea de salida y, en el centro, ocho paradas donde esperan una máquina de remo, un trineo de 152 kilos que empujar, unas pesas de 24 kilos, un saco de arena de 20 kilos que cargar a la espalda o una bola de seis kilos que lanzar al cielo. Entre estación y estación, un kilómetro de carrera. Así es una competición de Hyrox, la modalidad que en cinco años ha pasado de ser un experimento a mover 1,3 millones de participantes anuales en más de 85 ciudades de 30 países, entre ellos España.
Y no es la única del estilo. Deka, la prueba que combina correr y fuerza del grupo Spartan, está creciendo al mismo ritmo y ya está presente en 42 ciudades de 12 países, entre ellos también España. Athx, un formato parecido nacido recientemente en Reino Unido, acaba de firmar una alianza de cuatro años con Adidas para expandirse por todo el mundo. La Federación Española de Triatlón justo ha creado su formato híbrido, llamado Hyatlón, para entrar en el sector.
Y, junto a la aparición de decenas de pruebas locales, Red Bull, a su estilo, se ha inventado el cross kirolak, un híbrido con deportes tradicionales vascos. La moda no para de crecer y solo queda una pregunta: ¿es algo pasajero o es el inicio de un deporte nuevo?
Del barro al pabellón
El fenómeno responde a la unión de dos éxitos previos: de un lado, el running, deporte más practicado en España entre los adultos según los últimos datos del Ministerio de Educación, Formación Profesional y Deporte, y del otro, el crossfit y resto de actividades de gimnasio. Cardio y fuerza, la combinación perfecta; una apuesta segura que ya tenía un precedente. Hace más de una década, las carreras de obstáculos empezaron a ganar terreno en todo el mundo y abrieron la puerta a lo que vendría después. Una marca, Spartan, se hizo muy conocida antes incluso de aterrizar en España en 2014 y, con ella, llegaron las llamadas carreras híbridas.
"Nuestra mejor campaña de marketing fue la película 300", bromea María Gómez, directora general de Spartan y Deka Iberia, en conversación con EL MUNDO. La marca, aspiracional y de estética propia, arrasó en las capitales y, de hecho, hoy sigue organizando más de 250 carreras anuales en 65 países de todo el mundo. En paralelo nacían proyectos más locales, como Legion Race, fundada por Ricardo Calderón, exlegionario que trasladó al circuito los valores del entrenamiento militar en una finca de Barcelona con barro, cuerdas y fosas de agua. "Las tres bases de Legion Race son el reto, la superación y la diversión", resume Calderón, cuyo proyecto funciona con éxito año a año y prepara una expansión próxima a Madrid.
Las carreras de obstáculos siguen teniendo tirón y esperan un repunte con su incorporación como parte del pentatlón moderno en los Juegos Olímpicos de Los Ángeles 2028, pero les ha salido una feroz competencia. En 2017 nació Hyrox, fundada por tres directivos alemanes procedentes del hockey, el Ironman y de Audi que detectaron un hueco: no existía una competición simple y de escasa dificultad técnica para atraer al que corre y a quien va al gimnasio. El primer evento, en Hamburgo en 2018, reunió a 600 personas. El salto español llegó en 2021, en Madrid, con 1.600 inscritos y entradas agotadas dos semanas antes. Fue el pistoletazo de salida del 'boom' híbrido.
Similitudes y diferencias
Muchos son los motivos de su auge, pero uno es la estandarización. Hyrox repite el mismo formato -ocho kilómetros de carrera con ocho estaciones funcionales- en todos sus eventos, lo que permite comparar la marca de un participante en Barcelona con la de otro en Londres. Deka funciona de forma parecida, con distancias más cortas y más formatos de acceso.
"El público de Deka viene del fitness en general: hay entre 4,2 y 4,5 millones de practicantes de gimnasio, crossfit o entrenamiento funcional en España", explica Gómez. La marca ha crecido de forma exponencial en el país: de 4 eventos en 2023 a 15 este año, con más de 35.000 atletas frente a los 14.000 de 2024. Hyrox suele organizar pocos eventos, más exclusivos, y siempre en grandes ciudades, y Deka ha tomado el camino contrario: más carreras, inscripciones más baratas y presencia en ciudades medianas. Cada marca defiende su estrategia. "Podríamos hacer más, pero perdería un poco esa espera, esas ganas de decir: 'joder, me quedan cuatro meses para el Hyrox de Málaga, tengo que prepararme'", resume Álvaro del Busto, responsable de marketing de Hyrox Iberia, que pese a la competencia con Spartan coincide con Gómez en el componente social y visual de su deporte.
"Es muy instagrameable", admite Del Busto, que añade: "Hay un marketing potente en redes sociales, con contenido visual que genera FOMO y ganas de competir". Tanto Hyrox como Deka han conseguido crear una comunidad muy activa en redes sociales y han disparado el número de participantes femeninas hasta alcanzar o acercarse al 50%. "Las mujeres han perdido el miedo a levantar peso y eso es una muy buena noticia para la salud en general", subraya Gómez, que resalta que, precisamente por ese cambio de mentalidad, será difícil que las carreras híbridas pasen de moda.
El debate sobre si será un deporte consolidado, con practicantes en todo el mundo y pruebas fijas, tardará años en resolverse. Mientras tanto, miles de personas empujarán trineos y lanzarán bolas al aire cada fin de semana.

title: Indigenous fishers rethink shark hunting & protect species on Colombia’s coast
content:
- In the Colombian department of La Guajira, at South America’s northernmost tip, Indigenous Wayuu fishers from the community of Punta Gallinas are working with marine biologists to conserve and document shark populations.
- Despite a 2021 law banning targeted shark and ray fishing in Colombia, the meat remains a vital protein source in one of the country’s most remote and food-insecure regions.
- Colombian shark conservation initiative Proyecto Puyuii is working with Wayuu fishers to record shark species in the understudied waters of La Guajira, implementing sustainability measures such as larger-mesh nets, safe release techniques and avoiding longlines.
- With sustainable tourism touted as a potential economic alternative to shark fishing, some fishers argue that compensation will need to be offered before they can afford to stop.
LA GUAJIRA, Colombia — Feet from the ocean, four sharks and a ray lie dead on the wind-battered sand. Above them stands Wilfrido Arends, 46. The blade of a short knife glints in his hand.
Carefully, he bends down to cut a small fin from the underside of one shark — an endangered species known as a blacknose (Carcharhinus acronotus). He hands the sample to a woman next to him, who places it delicately in a vial.
A tape measure is passed over the still glistening back of the dead shark. Each measurement is read out and noted down.
Arends, a fisher from Colombia’s Wayuu Indigenous community, is spearheading shark research and conservation in Punta Gallinas, a Wayuu community where shark meat is part of the traditional diet. Home to around 50 families, the community sits at the northernmost tip of South America.
“If we wipe out our sharks, I think that further down the line we will miss them,” says Arends, who is known locally as “Caracas.”
Together with researchers from Colombian shark conservation initiative Proyecto Puyuii, Arends and other Wayuu fishers are documenting shark diversity in the largely unstudied waters of La Guajira.
“There’s almost no data on anything,” says Diego Cardeñosa, a marine biologist at Florida International University in the U.S. A member of Proyecto Puyuii, he has been training Wayuu fishers to record the shark species they catch.
A 2021 law banned shark and ray fishing in Colombia, with a 2024 revision subsequently allowing the incidental bycatch of 15 species. Despite the ban, the meat remains an important source of protein for Wayuu communities across this stretch of arid desert coast — one of the most food-insecure regions in the country.
While commercial poaching is the leading threat to shark populations in Colombia, biologists say that without additional research even traditional subsistence hunting can increase pressure on sharks, possibly affecting their numbers or threatening endangered species — as happened with overconsumption of turtles.
Proyecto Puyuii aims to promote economic alternatives for fishers, minimize pressure on the local shark population with scientific research and implement sustainable fishing practices.
The consumption of sharks is accepted by the project, as it is a traditional practice and form of subsistence. But directed shark fishing (generally practiced with longlines in the deeper ocean) is not encouraged. A more sustainable model would limit consumption to incidental bycatch, which depending on the species is not illegal, and include safe release techniques of juveniles.
“If the fisher earns more showing it than killing it, there’s the solution,” says Felipe González, who co-founded the project with Arends over a decade ago. “How do we make these sharks worth more alive than dead?”
‘I gave up shark-directed fishing many years ago’
Like many Wayuu boys in the region, Arends began fishing at the age of 9. As a child, he watched his grandparents hunt shark species ranging from hammerheads to tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier).
“As I got older I took to fishing them too, because it was a custom of the Wayuu,” says Arends, who recalls participating in a once booming trade that saw shark meat and fins exchanged for money, fuel or resources with buyers in neighboring Venezuela.
“You’d sell it and buy fuel to keep fishing,” he remembers. “We’d buy nets and hooks. That’s how we kept ourselves going.” At this time, fishers in Punta Gallinas would use artisanal longlines specialized for shark fishing, as well as finer-mesh gillnets that result in higher levels of shark bycatch. According to Arends, the trade began to disappear from Punta Gallinas over a decade ago, before vanishing from the community with the 2021 prohibition.
Local fishers told Mongabay that other Wayuu communities do still participate in a market, with buyers from the towns of Riohacha and Uribia paying around 50,000 Colombian pesos (about $15) per kilo for shark fins.
Though the fin trade is absent in Punta Gallinas, shark meat is still commonly consumed in the community, forming the key ingredient in a traditional dish known as salpicón. Oil is also extracted from the carcasses and used for cooking, while the liver is used in the production of a traditional cough medicine.
Whatever meat is not consumed by the fisher’s own family is typically sold to locally owned hotels and restaurants. Biologists have not assessed the mercury levels (which could be harmful at high concentrations) of shark meat in Punta Gallinas. González says it may be low and is currently not a concern of the project.
“It’s an important protein source,” Arends says, “the first source we have here to feed ourselves and our children is shark.”
Despite the ongoing subsistence use in his community, Arends is determined to promote shark conservation.
“Now I fish mostly with nets — I’ve stopped using what we call the longline, because that fishing is more directed at sharks,” he says. “I gave up shark-directed fishing many years ago.”
Since the early 2000s, Arends has worked on community-based mangrove and sea turtle conservation. Locals report that sea turtles, once a common sight, have disappeared from the area due to overconsumption in local Wayuu communities.
“What happened with the turtles — we don’t want the same thing to happen with the sharks,” he says.
He and other Punta Gallinas fishers began to use large-mesh nets to avoid catching juvenile sharks, focusing instead on other fish species by placing nets away from the open sea, where sharks are commonly found.
If he catches a shark incidentally, it will be released if found alive.
Locals report that these measures have been widely adopted in Punta Gallinas. And, according to Arends, around 17 boats out of an estimated 20 in the community no longer practice shark-directed fishing. Numbers aren’t available on how many have also changed to larger-mesh nets.
“You feel like your programming has been changed — from hunter to protector,” he says. “You feel almost the same as what the animals feel.”
‘A high concentration of shark species’
Though still largely understudied, biologists believe that the waters around Punta Gallinas are likely to contain a wealth of shark diversity.
“In La Guajira and other parts of the Colombian Caribbean, there appears to be a high concentration of ray and shark species,” says Camilo Garcia, professor of marine biology at the National University of Colombia, who mapped the distribution of sharks and rays across the Colombian Caribbean using research data from as far back as the 1960s.
Though his work identified a total of 90 species, he describes the inventory as “incomplete” and believes that further research is needed to establish sustainable catch levels and ensure the sustainability of current and future fishing practices.
In Punta Gallinas, Wayuu fishers have reported the presence of species ranging from tiger and silky sharks to endangered blacknose and the critically endangered smalleye hammerhead (Sphyrna tudes).
Cardeñosa believes that Proyecto Puyuii’s drive to document shark species is a crucial step toward facilitating more informed conservation measures in the future, such as fishing quotas and conservation areas.
As part of the project, Wayuu fishers measure every shark they catch, with dated fin samples passed to Arends for storage.
“This is going to give us a bigger picture of the species composition of the fishery, how much they’re catching and whether it can be sustainable,” Cardeñosa says. “Then we can start to formulate more advanced projects.”
‘What are we going to live off?’
Amid mounting food and water insecurity across La Guajira’s desert coast, a potential transition away from shark fishing is a challenging proposition for some communities. The Wayuu fishers Mongabay spoke to generally consider the 2021 law unfair on communities that still subsist on shark.
Locals report that a lack of rain in 2025’s wet season resulted in widespread plant and livestock death. Luzmila Arends, sister of Wilfrido, reports losing around 247 of her 300 goats after the failed rainy season left little vegetation to feed them. Goats are another common source of meat in Wayuu communities.
Meanwhile, one in three children in the region suffers from chronic malnutrition.
“Many people live off of shark meat,” says Juan Manuel Uriana, 33, leader of the fishers’ association in Bahía Hondita, a larger Wayuu community around 7 kilometers (about 4 miles) from Punta Gallinas. “Since there’s no other way for people to live, they do it to survive … they know it’s a crime now.”
According to Uriana, many of the 120 fishers in Bahía Hondita use hooks and longlines to catch sharks and rays, a trade they still rely on for survival.
“You have to compensate people. Then they would stop fishing shark,” he says. “What are we going to live off?”
Proyecto Puyuii members hope that sustainable tourism can provide alternative opportunities. The project is currently affiliated with a Wayuu-run hotel and kite surfing school in the area, a short drive from the famous Taroa sand dunes — a renowned beauty spot.
“The idea is that the money stays in the community,” González says, “that the tourist arrives, sleeps in their guesthouse, eats what they prepare, uses their boats and their guides.”
For some in Punta Gallinas, this has already become a reality.
“I’m earning more now,” says Alexi López, 56, uncle of Wilfrido Arends. Once one of Punta Gallinas’ most prolific shark fishers, he now makes most of his living driving cars and boats for tourists. “It’s easier [than fishing] because I go out, am done in two hours and am back home again.”
Luzmila Arends runs a local guesthouse, which offers visitors the chance to accompany fishers on boat outings.
She hopes that economically viable alternatives will help the community to shift away from a historical dependence on shark meat. “It’s all culture,” she says. “It’s not that we talk today and tomorrow it’s done, but that people go forwards with that vision for the future. It won’t happen overnight.”
‘Better we release them’
Even amongst those who live off shark fishing, there is evidence of a growing willingness to protect what remains.
“If this project works out, we can participate in conservation, we can work with this,” Uriana says. “The people are open to it.”
In May 2026, fishers in Bahía Hondita caught a large female tiger shark. On opening the animal, they found that it was pregnant. “One of the boys was going to gather [the pups] to take them away,” Uriana says. “I said: no, why are you going to take them? Better we release them.”
According to marine biologists, the protection of young sharks is of particular importance for a sustainable fishery. “More dangerous is fishing juveniles,” Garcia says. “If you catch them, especially before they’ve reproduced, you’re destroying the population directly.”
Using safe release techniques learned from Proyecto Puyuii, Uriana released 43 living tiger shark pups into the ocean.
He speaks from behind dark glasses and the low brim of a cap. “We started releasing them with the children,” he says.
A group of young boys, aged between 8 and 12, watches on as he talks. Uriana gestures to them. “They already know how to fish,” he says.
Back on his fishing boat, Wilfrido Arends scans the horizon, one hand guiding the onboard motor at the rear. A ragged black flag, marking the position of his net, appears from behind the crest of a wave.
Without a word, his 22-year-old son moves to haul it into the boat. He is nicknamed “Caraquitas” (“Little Caracas”) after his father.
“Everything we’ve tried to do is to leave something for our children,” says Arends, whose granddaughter and one of his sons want to become marine biologists. Arends, himself, dreams of one day establishing a shark research center in Punta Gallinas.
“Our ancestors have left this to us,” he says. “We want to leave something better for those who come next.”
